speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There are three sets of legislative changes contained in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This DEI scheme, which was introduced in 1997, is intended to encourage companies to grow capabilities and conduct new or expanded activities in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: It currently offers two concessionary tax rate tiers of 5% and 10%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This arises from our periodic review to ensure that our tax incentives remain relevant to companies with different circumstances and needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: For instance, a company affected by the global minimum effective tax rate of 15% might find the new 15% tax rate tier sufficient for its needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The second set of amendments expands the scope of companies eligible for a DEI award tenure of up to 40 years to include non-headquarter service companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Today, this feature is only available to headquarter companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The inclusion of non-headquarter service companies will provide flexibility for our economic agencies to support deserving companies that make long-term plans to develop capabilities and improve their service offerings from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Today, adjusting the qualifying project types under the Investment Allowance Scheme requires amending the main EEIA legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clauses 4 to 6 provide for the qualifying project types to be introduced, updated or removed via subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the two main changes in the amendment Bill relates to the DEI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The DEI allows businesses engaging in high value-added goods or services to apply for a certificate entitling them to a concessionary tax rate for the income from one or more qualifying activities stated in the certificate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, the concessionary tax rates on qualifying income may be 5% or 10%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What number and proportion of applications under the DEI have been granted a 5% concessionary tax rate and what number and proportion of applications have been granted a 10% concessionary tax rate?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is this change in light of the 15% floor on minimum effective tax rates under Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, am I correct to understand that the entities belonging to large MNE groups caught under Pillar Two will no longer be granted 5% or 10% concessionary tax rates under the DEI going forward?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what is the number and percentage of successful DEI applicants that such entities account for?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Considering that a 15% concessionary tax rate, even putting aside the prescribed 0.5% step-up during the tax relief period, is not too far from our statutory corporate income tax rate of 17%, is it necessary to create this new tier, as opposed to simply excluding all entities caught by Pillar Two from the DEI?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the flip side, does that mean that applicants who are not entities caught under Pillar Two, such as small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and smaller MNEs, can still expect to be granted the 5% and 10% concessionary tax rates as a norm?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And how much corporate tax have we effectively forgone from corporates through the DEI?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the qualifying fixed capital expenditure has so far been defined by reference to clearly circumscribed types of projects under the principal Act, the amendment Bill now seeks to add a sweep-up category of any project and related capital expenditure as may be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the amount of capital expenditure investment allowance that has been granted thus far and how are they broken down by project type and by expenditure categories?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be a broader exercise to review the list of qualifying project types against our strategic national priorities today, such as our green economy and the push to make it more AI- and data-centric?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From time to time, we have been amending and tweaking the Act to modify, add or remove the various incentives led by our agencies such as the Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, with Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0, there is now much less room for below-the-line tax incentives such as concessionary tax rates or deductions that potentially reduces a company's effective tax rate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not even taking into account the potential impact of Pillar One, which has not been implemented yet.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From a more macro level, how should we look to redesign our investment incentives and toolkit in this post-BEPS 2.0 world?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the involvement of various different Ministries and agencies, who would take the lead in this regard?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would be grateful for the Minister's insights on how we are going to do this and to assure Singaporeans that we will still be able to attract good companies to anchor themselves in Singapore and create good jobs and flow-on opportunities as a result.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead of a piecemeal adaptation of the Act, should we expect an overhaul in the form of a new, consolidated Act in the near future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in business, you ultimately cannot ignore the dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is imperative that we navigate how to give businesses the right monetary incentives while remaining true to our international commitments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding the clarification sought, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I spoke on the joint debate on the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Bill and associated Income Tax (Amendment) Bill then, as did my Sengkang teammate, Louis Chua.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I will offer some additional thoughts here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I will speak about the nature of incentives for corporations and more generally, about the principle of effective taxes on businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The overarching economic objective of incentives offered via tax breaks is to encourage firms to expand their investments and scale up their operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, this is targeted at high value-added products and services, and the pathway begins with, initially, schemes such as the Pioneer Certificate Incentive or Start-Up Tax Exemptions, which offer a tax holiday of three to five years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When this expires, it may be followed by the DEI, which grants a concessionary tax rate of between 5% and 15%, at least today, based on earnings that exceed the average of the prior three years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Schemes such as these have allowed Singapore to keep its effective tax rates (ETRs) relatively competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The rates that companies actually pay, rather than what on the face they owe, of course, are different, and in the case of the statutory tax rate, it has been in place at the 17% rate since 2010.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This need not be a bad thing per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Economists know that low taxes on capital promotes investment from both domestic and foreign sources, which, in turn, can drive growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is worth reflecting a little on why we accept this trade-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we do not willy-nilly grant tax relief to income on labour or land, believing that workers and landowners, rich and poor, should pay their fair share, at least in paying for the public goods that we all enjoy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, at least, we must be convinced that such tax reliefs generate benefits of additional investment that will lead to new jobs or create new competitive industries or yield greater opportunities for other companies that exceed the costs of the forgone tax revenue, which could have been directed to myriad other purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether these tax rates do so, however, is far from established.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, the Government does require that a certain number of jobs be created as qualifying conditions for these schemes, but it is not known whether these jobs would have been created anyway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor do we know if, in the absence of these incentives, there may have been some gaming of the criteria with temporary or ghost positions created to meet the conditions, only to be extinguished thereafter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would be curious to know if the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), or Ministry of Finance (MOF) for that matter, has ever conducted rigorous studies that show how low ETRs are causally linked to job creation or spillover effects and, if so, if they would be willing to share them with this House and the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: New legislation being passed around the world, such as our own Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Bill just passed last month, will now allow top-up taxes to be levied by other jurisdictions, should they view our effective taxes as unjustifiably low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The stipulations of BEPS, of course, only apply to the largest MNEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This offers some leeway for us to marginally improve the corporate tax environment for the corporations that are not among the largest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is where the present Bill plays an important role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, in my view, some aspects merit deeper questioning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sort of built-in deadlines to tax holidays, often referred to as sunset clauses, are now standard fare in public policy surrounding corporate tax incentives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, even special economic zones, the traditional preserve of tax freedom worldwide, have now begun to routinely incorporate sunset provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, it is crucial that sunset clauses not be prolonged indefinitely, because doing so could give rise to opportunities for politicking and quid pro quo rent-seeking, as firms lobby for extensions of special treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, the proposed amendments to section 41 include, under the definition of fixed capital expenditure, in Part 4A2, the "acquisition of know-how or patent rights".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand the motivation behind why one might wish to include such expenses as part of fixed capital, the immediate concern is that this could be used as a loophole to creatively transfer existing intangible assets from one corporate entity to another as a means of reducing taxable income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sort of potential abuse in transfer pricing was, after all, one of the motivating drivers of the BEPS project to begin with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It would be ironic if our laws inadvertently provided yet another reason for countries to accuse us of seeking a role as a tax haven, albeit on the smaller scale than the MNEs covered by BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, I observe that there is a distinctive treatment of the conditions associated with accessing concessionary tax rates when it comes to manufacturing versus services, at least as documented in the existing DEI literature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, while the equivalent qualifying expenditures for the latter group are the same in the fifth year, it adds further requirements that $8 million be invested and 18 skilled employees be hired by the third year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will be helpful to understand the justification between this disparate treatment of the two sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is welcome because, as I shared last month, we really should be weaning ourselves off a growth model that is excessively reliant on foreign capitals and MNEs and moving towards one that is conducive to entrepreneurship and supporting the development of homegrown SMEs as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, MNEs benefit disproportionately more than SMEs from the public goods provided by the taxpayer, our favourable business environment, safe domestic market for skilled labour and stable political climate and have the necessary resources to contribute back towards sustaining the system that they have benefited so much from.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We need not fear making these companies pay their fair share, given how their location decisions are driven primarily by the availability of skilled workers, open economic borders, high quality transportation infrastructure and a sound institutional environment, and only secondarily by low taxes on corporate income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, we need to help our small firms which are struggling under the burden of high and rising costs, especially as rising rental costs on land snuff out affordable factory facilities and office spaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when the high costs of living are eventually transmitted into durable increases in real wages, these firms will also need to manage their ongoing costs of running their businesses amidst a small, cost-conscious domestic consumer market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tax relief will give them a genuine shot at growing and perhaps flourishing in the long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is an outcome that I am certain all of us in this House would look forward to seeing and for this reason, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments to the Bill not only align Singapore's tax policies with global trends, but also reinforce our status as a competitive business hub amidst shifting international standards.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As jurisdictions worldwide compete for investments through tax incentives, we must ensure our policies remain competitive and compliant with international norms, such as the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development's guidelines fostering both economic resilience and sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments also encourage foreign investment supporting economic growth through favourable tax incentives for strategic industries, such as finance and logistics.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments support companies involved in regional operations qualifying development projects and capital investments through targeted tax relief.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, clause 3 of the Bill also extends tax relief periods for eligible projects up to the end of 2028, ensuring sustained support for businesses expanding in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also applaud provisions in the Bill supporting innovation and infrastructure growth with amendments to the capital expenditure allowance which will encourage businesses to invest in new technologies, infrastructure and high-tech industries by widening the scope of eligible activities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, this allows Singapore to position itself as a global leader in high-tech industries.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, by streamlining tax relief frameworks, these amendments provide legal clarity and ease of planning, empowering businesses to pursue growth with confidence.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: First, will companies benefiting from existing incentives need to reapply under the new framework or will their current exemptions automatically continue?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Second, since BEPS 2.0 primarily targets large multinational enterprises, what specific benefits will SMEs gain from these amended tax incentives and how will they remain competitive in this new environment?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Third, under clause 2 of the Bill, are specific thresholds in place for qualifying for the 15% tax rate, particularly for companies managing regional operations?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, how will the new amendments align with Singapore's international tax treaties to prevent double taxation and support cross-border activities?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, what penalties will be imposed for non-compliance with milestone-based relief provisions and will there be an appeals process for this?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly pressing as the global minimum tax rules take place in various jurisdictions, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed Economic Expansion Incentives Bill introduces enhancements to Singapore's tax framework, specifically targeting the DEI and Investment Allowances for eligible companies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These refinements aim to drive economic growth by supporting business development, innovation and investment, ultimately strengthening resilience and competitiveness in a shifting global landscape.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is applicable to qualifying income derived on or after 1 January 2024.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging to see the Government respond very proactively by introducing changes to existing suite of tax incentives to ensure their relevance as part of the overall economic support package to attract foreign investments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is useful as it provides certainty to businesses and allows them to plan their operations and apply for the tier of incentive tax rate which is most suitable for their business.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This flexibility is commendable as it acknowledges the financial volatility that businesses may face.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, I recommend clear guidance be issued as to the process or application timeline for such rate substitutions as it would ensure that the system operates smoothly and avoids potential confusion among businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For the Investment Allowance scheme, or IA, the amendments enable the Minister to prescribe projects in relation to which the IA may be given in regulations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This means that there is greater upfront clarity as to whether a particular project can qualify for the IA.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, while broadening the eligibility scope is positive, can the Ministry clarify the timeline and criteria for such inclusions?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will allow companies greater certainty when planning investments in sectors not traditionally supported by investment allowances.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By providing flexible and targeted tax incentives, we can continue to attract diverse businesses that contribute to Singapore's economic dynamism.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my questions and recommendations, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's attractiveness for FDIs is underpinned by our robust legal framework, skilled workforce, political stability, excellent transportation system and world-class infrastructure, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our tax incentive frameworks, including the Pioneer Incentive and DEI, give us a competitive edge to attract companies looking to build capabilities globally.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last month, in this Chamber, during the debate on the Income Tax Bill and Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Bill, we extensively discussed the increasing global competition to attract investments, the minimum effective tax rates, the importance of continued investments in Singapore and ensuring that MNEs comply with BEPS 2.0 requirements.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Economic Expansion Incentive Bill further strengthens our investment toolkit by introducing significant enhancements to Singapore's tax incentive framework, something which has also been mentioned by Member Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, in clauses 2 and 3, the amendments to section 21 add an additional layer of concessionary tax rates, which is a welcome enhancement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Depending on the structure, companies may not find the current two tax tiers of 5% or 10% useful.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thus, some companies affected by the minimum ETR may still find the 15% rate valuable in developing their capabilities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When building new capabilities, the required infrastructure has become increasingly specialised, especially when requirements for particulate control, flatness of building and temperature and humidity regulation are required in the project.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The rising building costs in Singapore, which has increased by over 30% in some cases post-COVID-19, has exacerbated these challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, the inclusion of capital expenditure on structures specially designed for carrying out the project as a qualifying expense is much appreciated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, this will attract companies developing industrialised solutions for additive manufacturing of exotic metals, like titanium, for the medical and aerospace industries or creating quantum computing solutions based on acquired IPs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Including productive equipment to be used outside of Singapore within the investment framework also reflects the realities of today's supply chains, where value streams often span multiple jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This provision allows labour-intensive work in partner countries, while Singapore focuses on higher-value tasks, benefiting our workforce through upskilling and creating high-value jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, I have several points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What criteria will overseas investments need to meet to qualify as allowable fixed capital expenditure?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Bill also grants the Minister authority to define the list of qualifying business activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the criteria for determining these qualifying activities and how often will this list be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They spoke about the DEI and Investment Allowance schemes, and on the need for a holistic review of our investment attraction toolkit to ensure Singapore remains attractive to global investors in a post-BEPS world.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Allow me to start, first, with the DEI scheme.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The first set of questions relate to the DEI's new 15% concessionary tax rate tier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The questions surround whether we need this when it is not too far from our current corporate income tax rate of 17% or if this responds to the 15% minimum ETR under Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0 and how will SMEs or the awards of existing in-scope DEI recipients be affected?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat rightly noted that the in-scope MNE groups will be subject to the minimum ETR of 15% under Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0 and that the difference between the new 15% DEI concessionary tax rate and our statutory corporate income tax rate of 17% is, in fact, narrow.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We made these changes as part of our periodic review to ensure our incentives continue to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Notwithstanding the narrow differences in the tax rates, we have received industry feedback, for instance, that a company affected by the global minimum ETR of 15% under Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0 might find the new 15% tier sufficient for their needs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The new 15% tier may also be useful to other companies, which may only be able to make economic commitments at a level commensurate with this new 15% concessionary tax rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Sakthiandi Supaat also asked if SMEs and smaller MNEs could still expect to be granted the DEI of 5% and the 10% concessionary tax rates as a norm.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This also applies to the new DEI of 15% concessionary tax rate tier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked if companies benefiting from the existing incentives need to re-apply under this new framework.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The second set of questions relate to the use of DEI.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: What criteria or thresholds are applied to determine whether a business is granted a 5%, 10% or 15% tier, and what are the number and proportion of DEI recipients enjoying the 5% and 10% concessionary tiers?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our economic philosophy, Mr Speaker, has always been to support all companies that can bring value to Singapore and to have the incentivised companies commit to generating economic contributions to Singapore that are commensurate with the incentive benefit that they enjoy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is regardless of where they come from, their country of origin or their size.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We systematically assess each application for a new DEI award or the amendment to an existing award considering the merits of each and every case.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To be eligible for DEI, the company must engage in high-value-added activities in Singapore, either through a new set-up or if they decide to expand existing activities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Economic agencies will then assess the new or updated project, based on the scale of the project and the projected quantitative and qualitative economic benefits.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Quantitative economic benefits include skilled employment, fixed asset investment and total business expenditure committed under the project.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Qualitative benefits include the generation of spin-offs for the economy, the quality of jobs created from the project and the commitment to grow capabilities in technology, skillsets and know-how in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Based on projected economic commitments by the company, we will then grant the DEI recipient a commensurate concessionary tax rate in respect of its qualifying activities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Of course, because the new concessionary tax rate tier is new, we will not yet be able to assess the expected take-up rate of this new DEI 15% concessionary tax rate tier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But we are introducing this new tier to continue to anchor new investment commitments amid the tight global competition for investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The third set of questions relate to the governance of the DEI awards.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Mark Lee suggested having clear guidance on the process or an application timeline for rate substitution to ensure its smooth implementation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, this practice of rate substitution is not new.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Existing DEI recipients can approach economic agencies to discuss any changes in their circumstances and also the impact on their incentive award.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For instance, where there are changes in the global business landscape or climate, or if there were shifts in industry trends or corporate restructuring, a company may then need to make changes to their project deliverables.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is over the course of doing business.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This may warrant then a reexamination of the tax incentive and the conditions tied to the tax incentives, which may involve a change in the concessionary tax rate to ensure, again, that the tax benefits remain commensurate with the scale and the impact of the incentivised project.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi and Mr Mark Lee also mentioned the extension of the DEI scheme until the end of 2028, also a point that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Mark Lee suggested periodically reviewing the sunset dates to ensure the incentive remains relevant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Government measures DEI efficacy and the corporate tax, which we have forgone through DEI.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also asked about this forgone tax.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are amending the sunset date to align with the rest of the DEI scheme in general, which is already 31 December 2028.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I would like to assure Members who have asked this question that we review our incentives periodically to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But this is a point to ensure that these are aligned to the existing 31 December 2028 dates.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This includes the estimated incremental value-add that the scheme is projected to create and the incremental economic commitments such as skilled employment, fixed asset investments and business expenditure that the supported projects can anchor here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: DEI is not automatically granted to all companies looking to invest in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Instead, it is offered judiciously, only if our economic agencies assess that the incentive is crucial to land the investment here and that the investment will generate a net benefit for Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In other words, we assess how effective the tax incentive is based on benefits brought forth by the project, for example, the number of good jobs created, and if not for the incentives, whether the investment may land here in the first place.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Neil Parekh asked about penalties that will be imposed for non-compliance with milestone-based relief provisions and if there is an appeals process.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I wanted to assure Members that the Government maintains a high bar in terms of the commitments we expect from recipients of these incentives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Where there is a breach of incentive conditions, we will give the company an opportunity to show cause and explain reasons for the breach.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And if there are no strong justifications and the intended economic benefits are not realised, we will hold the incentive recipients accountable and not hesitate to either amend or withdraw the incentive, including clawing back the benefits enjoyed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To Mr Neil Parekh's question on aligning our amendments to Singapore's international tax treaties to prevent double taxation and cross-border activities, I wish to affirm that the proposed amendments do not affect the application of the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreements that Singapore has signed with other countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore has been and will continue to be committed to fulfilling our international commitments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This trust factor is a key value proposition for companies investing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Sharael Taha sought clarification on the criteria for an overseas investment to qualify as allowable fixed capital expenditure and the asset retention requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Typically, the productive equipment that is incentivised under the Investment Allowance scheme is to be used in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That could be a plant, for example, or productive equipment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The only exceptions to this are space satellite and submarine cable systems, as these need to be obviously deployed outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To qualify for Investment Allowance, the company must hold onto the incentivised equipment for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if we will review the list of qualifying project types against our current strategic national priorities, such as our green economy, data as well as our AI ambitions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And as Members suggest, given that we have plans to use AI to transform our economy and also our push for a green economy, we are happy and open to consider the Investment Allowance scheme as a potential incentive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, this could be in the form of jobs created or new partnerships with local suppliers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The short answer is we are doing so to give the Government greater flexibility to respond to the rapidly changing economic landscape by providing for qualifying project types to be introduced, updated or removed via subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It allows for the Minister to move quicker in a rapidly evolving space.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked about the amount of capital expenditure investment allowance we have granted thus far and the breakdown by project type and by expenditure categories.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Similar to the DEI, the Investment Allowance is offered judiciously and we consider any taxable income forgone by the Investment Allowance award to be notional in nature, as I mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The value of the capital expenditure Investment Allowance that has been awarded is a fraction of the total projected value of investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will now address Members' questions on the need for a holistic review of our investment attraction toolkit to ensure Singapore remains attractive to global investments in a post-BEPS world.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Although BEPS 2.0's Pillar Two may reduce the room for tax competition amongst countries, it does not reduce competition for investment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The global economic landscape has become even more competitive, with major economies like the US, Germany and Japan rolling out generous incentives to attract investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, to ensure our incentive schemes remain relevant and competitive, both MTI and MOF have been continuously refreshing our incentive toolkits and updating legislations under our purview as required.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This is one arrow in our quiver, in our toolkit, to ensure that our incentives have enough levers and to ensure Singapore's continued economic relevance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is a process to ensure that we, as the economic agencies and the Government, will review our incentive schemes periodically.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It also sends a message to the businesses to not take for granted that the incentives will continue perpetually.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The alignment to other DEI schemes in general is important for us to do that.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The question on the difference in incentives criteria for both manufacturing and services is a good one.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Manufacturing, as the Member would know, and services are very different.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Our incentive design takes into consideration the competitive landscape we face and the gestation periods of the respective project types.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you think about manufacturing, a manufacturing company typically takes years to set up a plant, to qualify and to hire relevant workers and also to train their workers for these relevant skills, and then, later on, to ramp up operations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The level of commitment required also recognises, in part, the competition that Singapore faces.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think, in MTI, we open many of these plants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We know that there is a gestation period and these companies need to hire workers, train them and make sure that the plant is operational.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: You compare this with the manufacturing sector, for example, to our global headquarters as well as the services sector, the typical project gestation period is much shorter, because you do not need to have those plants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is not as sticky in that regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Purely shifting assets around would not pass muster with our robust assessment framework.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore's attractiveness as an investment location does not only depend on tax factors or incentives to anchor investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These advantages took decades to build and strengthen and are the result of consistent efforts by the Government working alongside businesses and our tripartite partners to create a vibrant and competitive economy for our people.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There has been fragmentation, there has been fractures of what we knew as the trading system, and just because of all of these factors, the global competition for talent, the global competition for investments is heating up, if it is not already at very intense levels.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have very limited resources, we have constraints, land, labour, carbon and, for all the strengths that we have – a well-connected financial system, highly educated workforce and the likes – which I mentioned earlier on, these are things that are important strengths and levers that we have.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, at the same time, we cannot take for granted, because we are small, that MNCs which have a choice to invest their plants or their services or to situate their headquarters anywhere in the world, will choose Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why we must be on the forward footing, we must continuously be agile-minded and agile-footed and amend, change, and be flexible with our suite of tools that are available to us to attract these investments into Singapore and to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I thank Members for their strong support for this Bill and Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first, if I could verify that the DEI is in fact not automatically granted to any company that commits to meet the qualifying conditions, for example, for the 5% bar, S$13 million additional foreign asset investment and 30 additional skilled workers, but actually is subject to clearance by staff at MTI?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if so, and if it is possible, to share the success rate of applicants to the DEI in the past or relatedly, how many successful applicants have subsequently experienced termination of the incentive for not meeting the terms of their letter of agreement (LOA) commitments?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or perhaps, if I should file a Parliamentary Question if these numbers are not immediately available?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Then, you adjust it, commensurate to the incentive.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any more clarifications for Minister of State Alvin Tan?
